extracted.intended_audience: parents/guardians and tutors of young gentlemen (nobility gentry) seeking guidance on education
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive advice for selecting and directing a tutor and for the overall upbringing and education of a boy of quality, emphasising judgment, practice, moral formation, travel, conversation, and physical hardening over rote book-learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a tutor with a 'well-made' head ('tete bien faite')
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek a tutor who is 'well-made' rather than merely 'well-filled' — prefer manners and judgment to mere learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: prefer a man with good judgment and manners over one stuffed with learning; seek both if possible but give precedence to temper and capacity to form the pupil. The tutor should exercise a new method rather than repeating common pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a dialogic/socratic method: make the pupil speak
rubrics_metrics.description: The tutor should put the pupil to the test by permitting him to taste things and to speak; scholars should be made to speak first, then the tutor speaks to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the common practice of 'pouring into a funnel' — instead, have the pupil try, open the way for him, and sometimes leave him to open it himself. Referenced models: Socrates, Arcesilaus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust teaching pace to the pupil's capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach as one would make a young horse trot before judging its going; accommodate the teacher's speed to the pupil's vigour and capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know how to proportion instruction and to condescend to childish motions; failing to adjust spoils all. This skill is hard and is a sign of a well-tempered soul.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid one-size-fits-all instruction for mixed-ability groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not instruct several boys of differing capacities with the same lesson and measure of direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When one master uses the same regimen for many unequal pupils, few profit — only two or three may benefit. Tailor instruction to individual abilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge a pupil's progress by life and understanding, not rote memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess profit not by testimony of memory but by how the pupil applies knowledge in life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make him put what he has learned into a hundred different forms and subjects to test true comprehension (Plato's pedagogic institutions). Rote retention without transformation is 'no knowledge'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require active transformation of learned material
rubrics_metrics.description: The pupil should alter the form and condition of what is learned — digest, not disgorge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: stomach must concoct food; likewise the mind must transform borrowed materials into its own judgment and output (bees making honey from various flowers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach critical examination; accept nothing on mere authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the pupil examine and thoroughly sift everything he reads; lodge nothing upon simple authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose him to diverse opinions (Aristotle, Epicurus, Stoics) so he can choose or remain in doubt if unable. Avoid blind adherence to any authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage intellectual independence: 'let him know that he knows'
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the pupil imbibes knowledge to apply it, rather than be corrupted by precepts or slavishly follow authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It matters not that he forgets where he learned something if he can apply it himself. Truth is common; making knowledge one's own is the aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster originality by recombining borrowed fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the pupil to transform and shuffle borrowed fragments into a work that becomes absolutely his own judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should compile and rework sources so the product is their own; living on 'pillage and borrowing' exposes one to view without claiming sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value conversation and travel for practical learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use conversation with diverse people and travel abroad to learn humours, manners, customs, and laws rather than trivial measurements or curiosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel should sharpen wits by rubbing them against those of others; send abroad into nations with differing languages early to acquire flexibility in speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not raise the boy solely in his mother's lap; avoid over-tenderness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mothers' natural affection often prevents fitting correction and exposure to hardships necessary for useful adult capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A boy meant to be 'good for anything' must not be spared when young; must be allowed to get dusty, sweat, take cold drink when hot, mount unruly horses, fence, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strengthen the body as well as the soul; inure to labour and pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Make his sinews strong as well as fortify his soul — habit of labour hardens against pain and prepares him for misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise, exposure to discomfort, and roughness train the body to support the soul; prepare him for dislocations, cholics, cauteries, even imprisonment or rack as possible misfortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve tutor's sovereign authority free from parental interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The governor's authority should not be checked by parents' presence or by the pupil's knowledge of family status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family respect, knowledge of inheritance, or parental presence can impede the governor's capacity to discipline and form the boy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train modesty and silence in conversation; be sparing of knowledge-display
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the boy to be modest, sparing, and to husband his knowledge; avoid carping and reproving on every idle saying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Silence and modesty are advantageous; refrain from condemning everything not to one's palate; correct oneself rather than constantly faulting others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected or uncivil displays of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Let him avoid vain images of authority and childish ambition to appear better bred by ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only great poets may take poetical licence; ordinary men should not assume privileges beyond custom. Such affectations reveal weakness, not excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach selectivity and brevity in argument; scorn impertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruct him to engage in discourse only with worthy opponents, choose reasons carefully, abominate impertinence, and affect brevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He should not use every subtleness that fits his purpose but only arguments that serve him; learn to acquiesce to truth and to abandon unjust arguments (recantation is allowed and wise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form loyalty to public duty but avoid courtier dependency
rubrics_metrics.description: Form his will to be loyal to his prince and stout in quarrel but cool the desire for private ties that corrupt freedom of judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being a pure courtier corrupts freedom and dazzles judgment; avoid obligations that blind independent thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value conscience and sincerity; acknowledge errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Make conscience and virtue manifest in speech; teach that acknowledging one's error is an effect of judgment and sincerity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obstinacy and contention are traits of mean souls; revising oneself in dispute is rare and philosophic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be observant and learn from all ranks of people
rubrics_metrics.description: In company keep eye and ear active; learn from peasants, bricklayers, passengers — there is something to learn in every capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great honours often go to people with least in them; attention to lower conversations can reveal fine things missed by the ostentatious. Even folly contributes to instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage an inquisitive curiosity about singular things and places
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggest an honest curiosity: see fine houses, fountains, battle-sites, passages of great men; inquire into manners, revenues, and alliances of princes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let him go see whatever is singular and rare nearby; such inquiries are pleasant and useful to know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use history to converse with great souls and to learn manners, not dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach history so the pupil converses with heroic souls; focus on manners and reasons behind actions rather than mere narrative dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer Plutarch for anatomy of philosophy; teach why Marcellus's death was dishonourable rather than when it occurred. Avoid treating history as grammar alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with those studies that regulate manners and self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritise instruction that makes one free and teaches to know oneself, how to live, what is to be wished and what to avoid, before abstruse sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit the course of studies to true and real utility (following Socrates). Teach valour, temperance, justice, difference between ambition/avarice, servitude/subjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid teaching impractical or premature subjects (e.g., astrology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not waste time on matters like the stars or learned trivialities before attending to present, pressing enemies of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Anaximenes' admonition: puzzling over celestial secrets is pointless when death or slavery threatens; focus on practical ends first.

rubrics_metrics.name: After moral formation, introduce formal elements (logic, physics, geometry, rhetoric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once judgment is formed by practical instruction, entertain him with elements of formal sciences according to his inclinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach the elements sometimes by discourse, sometimes by reading; sometimes give full authors, sometimes summaries. If the governor lacks required learning, join a learned man to supply occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present philosophy as pleasant and life-enhancing; virtue is joyful and accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that philosophy is cheerful, eases the soul, fosters serene confidence; virtue consists in the facility, utility, and pleasure of its exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combat the false, grim image of philosophy: it calms storms of soul, teaches moderation. Teach virtue by order not force; moderation makes pleasures pure and permanent.
